questions.question: Explain how the Earth's rotation causes day and night and the apparent movement of the sun across the sky. Calculate the approximate speed of rotation at the equator, given a circumference of about 40 000 km.
questions.expected_answer: The Earth rotates on its axis from west to east once every 24 hours. At any moment half the Earth faces the sun and has day while the other half has night, divided by the circle of illumination. As the Earth turns, places move into the light at sunrise and out of it at sunset. Because the Earth turns towards the east, the sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west. Speed at the equator: 40 000 ÷ 24 is about 1 670 km/h.

questions.question: Show how the figures of 15° per hour and 4 minutes per degree are derived. Two towns are 13° of longitude apart; what is the difference in their local solar time, and which town is ahead?
questions.expected_answer: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so 360 ÷ 24 = 15° per hour. One hour is 60 minutes, so 60 ÷ 15 = 4 minutes per degree. A difference of 13° gives 13 × 4 = 52 minutes. The town further east is ahead, because it turns into the sunlight first.

questions.question: Explain what SAST is and why the whole of South Africa uses one time zone. When it is 14:00 SAST, what is the time in Tokyo, at UTC plus nine, and in New York in its winter, at UTC minus five?
questions.expected_answer: SAST is South African Standard Time, UTC plus two hours, based on the 30°E meridian. The country uses one time zone for convenience in business, transport, broadcasting and government, even though it stretches from about 16°E to 33°E, so the sun's highest point in Cape Town comes about three-quarters of an hour after noon on the clock. Tokyo is seven hours ahead of SAST, so it is 21:00. New York in winter is seven hours behind SAST, so it is 07:00.
